one_line: Single-run tests of Claude Opus 5 against Fable 5, GPT 5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 on one-shot app builds plus benchmarks: Opus leads on UI and agentic scores, but its cost per run is close to Fable's.
summary: Better Stack reviews Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 release, leaning on vendor-reported and third-party benchmarks (ARC-AGI, Artificial Analysis, Cursor Bench) before running its own tests. The benchmark story is strong: Opus 5 scores 30.2% on ARC-AGI and leads the Artificial Analysis agentic and Intelligence indexes, and it is second on the coding index. Its per-token price matches Opus 4.8 at $5 input and $25 output per million tokens. The presenter then gives each of four models (Opus 5, Fable 5, GPT 5.6 Sol, Kimi K3) the same one-shot prompts: a single-file F1 racing game and a full-stack personal finance dashboard. He ranks Opus 5 best on the F1 game and on dashboard UI, while GPT 5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 show weaker results (a broken track, a JSON file in place of a database). Cost is the weak point for Opus: it used about five times the tokens on the F1 task, costing about $12.99 by his estimate, more than Fable, and on the finance test it cost $29.82 against Fable's $30.79 and took longer. Cost figures come from Claude Code's usage tool, not billing. The video concludes that Opus 5 can replace Fable for most work, while Fable may still be better for very long-horizon problems, and that GPT models are much cheaper. It is two runs per model and the presenter says so.
speakers: Better Stack host (name not stated in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: Opus 5 is positioned as close to Fable 5's frontier intelligence at lower price and is the new default on Claude Max.
key_ideas.detail: Presenter quotes the vendor description: it is designed for everyday use and works more efficiently than other models. Fable 5 is not in the ARC-AGI results because of Fable's data-retention terms, which the ARC-AGI team wanted to avoid. Opus 5 has no such retention requirement for general access.

key_ideas.idea: Opus 5 posts a large jump on ARC-AGI and reportedly used a new reasoning approach.
key_ideas.detail: It scores 30.2%, against 1.5% for Opus 4.8 and 7.8% for the previous high (a model the presenter calls Sol). The ARC-AGI team reportedly saw it rewrite puzzles in algebraic notation to reason through them. This is a reported observation, not something the presenter verified.

key_ideas.idea: On third-party indexes Opus 5 leads agentic and overall intelligence, and is second on coding.
key_ideas.detail: On the Artificial Analysis coding index it is 0.3 points behind GPT 5.6 Sol (extra high) and 1.5 points ahead of Fable 5. It takes the agentic index and the Intelligence Index.

key_ideas.idea: Cost per completed task is the more useful price comparison, not per-token list price.
key_ideas.detail: On Artificial Analysis cost-to-complete, Opus 5 costs about 72 cents less per task than Fable 5 and slightly more than Opus 4.8. On Cursor Bench, Opus 5 Max and Fable 5 score nearly the same, at about $8 and $17 per task. The presenter says GPT 5.6 Sol is the best price-performance, at nearly half Opus 5's cost.

key_ideas.idea: Single-shot F1 game: Opus 5 produced the best result, with no external assets.
key_ideas.detail: The prompt asks for a complete F1 racing game in one HTML file using 3GS (likely Three.js, an auto-caption error). Opus 5 gets the track, lap timing, positioning, collisions and gravel traps working. Fable 5 is also functional with simpler cars. GPT 5.6 Sol has a track that breaks partway round. Kimi K3 is close to GPT 5.6 Sol.

key_ideas.idea: Opus 5 used about five times the tokens on the F1 task, which made it more expensive than Fable.
key_ideas.detail: It took 46 minutes 51 seconds and cost about $12.99 at API prices by the presenter's estimate. Costs were calculated from Claude Code's usage tool, which may differ from real billing. The presenter hopes this is an outlier, since the other benchmarks do not show it.

key_ideas.idea: Full-stack finance dashboard: Opus 5 wins on UI and stack choices, and each model shows different architecture habits.
key_ideas.detail: Opus 5 uses React with React Router, node:sqlite and Express, and has the best UI. Fable 5 uses the same database and server but builds its own router, and its charts are weaker. GPT 5.6 Sol uses Next.js, Drizzle, and Cloudflare with Vinext hosting, puts features on one page, and the presenter suspects the prompt forced the Cloudflare stack. Kimi K3 builds its own router and stores data in a JSON file instead of a database.

key_ideas.idea: On the finance test, Opus 5 and Fable 5 cost nearly the same, and Opus took longer.
key_ideas.detail: Fable 5 cost $30.79 and took 56 minutes 55 seconds. Opus 5 cost $29.82 and took 59 minutes 15 seconds. The presenter says GPT models are about three and a half times cheaper.

key_ideas.idea: Opus 5 is less restrictive than Fable 5 on cybersecurity, but still blocks some tasks.
key_ideas.detail: It can find vulnerabilities in source code but blocks binary-based vulnerability scanning, penetration testing and exploit generation. The vendor reports that its classifiers intervene about 85% less often than for Fable 5. The presenter does not verify this.

techniques.name: Compare models on cost per completed task, not per-token price
techniques.how: Use Artificial Analysis cost-to-complete or a per-task cost such as Cursor Bench, and read the per-task cost next to the score. Do not assume the per-token price predicts run cost: here Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 had the same list price, yet Opus 5 used about five times the tokens on one task.
techniques.when: Choosing a default model for agent or coding workloads, or writing a cost estimate for a routing policy.

techniques.name: Estimate a subscription-billed run's cost from usage data
techniques.how: Run the task, read the token and time totals from Claude Code's usage tool, then convert to API-equivalent cost. The presenter notes this is approximate and may not match real billing.
techniques.when: You need cost comparisons on subscription plans where exact per-request billing is not shown. Label the figures as estimates.

techniques.name: One-shot app bake-off
techniques.how: Send the same single prompt to each model: one self-contained HTML file for a game (no external assets), or a full-stack app with a list of named features. Time each run, record cost, then run the output and check each feature by hand. Judge UI, stack choice, persistence (real DB or JSON file) and whether features are on separate pages.
techniques.when: Quick qualitative comparison of models on open-ended builds. With one run per model, treat results as directional, not as a benchmark.

techniques.name: Check whether the prompt or the model chose the stack
techniques.how: Before crediting or blaming a model for its stack (framework, hosting, database), check your prompt for hosting or framework instructions. The presenter suspects the GPT run's Cloudflare/Vinext stack was prompted.
techniques.when: Comparing models on generated architectures, to separate model defaults from prompt effects.

numbers.claim: Opus 5 scores 30.2% on ARC-AGI, against 1.5% for Opus 4.8 and 7.8% for the previous high.
Opus 5 is about 10% better than Fable 5 on FrontierBench (vendor claim).
Opus 5 is 0.3 points behind GPT 5.6 Sol (extra high) on the Artificial Analysis coding index and 1.5 points ahead of Fable 5.
Opus 5 costs about 72 cents less per task than Fable 5 on Artificial Analysis cost-to-complete, and slightly more than Opus 4.8.
Opus 5 pricing is $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, the same as Opus 4.8.
On Cursor Bench, Opus 5 Max scores about the same as Fable 5, at about $8 per task against $17 for Fable.
F1 single-file game: Opus 5 took 46m51s and cost about $12.99 at API prices (estimate), using about 5x more tokens than the other runs.
Finance dashboard: Fable 5 cost $30.79 and took 56m55s. Opus 5 cost $29.82 and took 59m15s.
GPT models are about 3.5x cheaper than Opus 5 on the finance test (presenter's estimate).
Opus 5 classifiers intervene about 85% less often than Fable 5 on cyber tasks (vendor testing).

hot_takes: The headline 'half the price' is not supported by the presenter's own data. The transcript gives no Fable per-token price, the per-task figures show a smaller gap (72 cents less per AA task, $8 vs $17 on one Cursor Bench task), and on the finance test Opus cost roughly the same as Fable.
The presenter contradicts himself on price: 'half the price' in the intro, then 'a third of the price' when discussing Artificial Analysis cost-to-complete.
Evidence is two single-run tests judged by eye, with costs estimated from a usage tool. The presenter says so, but the video still closes with a firm 'use Opus for 95% of work' verdict.
Benchmark and safety claims (ARC-AGI reasoning, FrontierBench, the 85% classifier figure) are vendor or third-party claims that the video does not check.
No sponsorship is seen in the transcript. Quality rests on the hands-on tests, which are useful but narrow.

relevance.why: AgentOS strategy routing and budget tracking depend on per-task cost. This video shows that the same task can use 5x more tokens on a different model, so per-token price alone is misleading for routing.
relevance.action: Add cost per completed task next to per-token price in the model-routing cost table, and record tokens per task, not just per request.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs Claude Code on checkpointed long runs. Usage-tool cost estimates are the same kind of approximation the presenter relies on, so the harness needs its own per-run totals.
relevance.action: Log input and output token totals and time per checkpointed run in ProsHarness, so cost per run can be compared across Claude models without relying on the subscription usage view.
